column1: A. Baseline paper (Almeida et al., 2011): how it supports our SVM baseline, and its limits

column2: A public English SMS corpus (5,574 messages, 13.40% spam) and a comparison of 14 classifier entries. Linear SVM + tok1 was best by MCC (0.893), catching 83.10% of spam and blocking 0.18% of ham, with 97.64% accuracy. The best four classifiers were not statistically different.

column1: How it supports TF-IDF + linear SVM
column2: It supports a linear SVM as a strong, simple baseline on short messages with sparse token features and no dimensionality reduction, and it models the habit of reporting blocked ham next to accuracy.

It does not describe TF-IDF weighting in the text read (it uses two tokenizers and WEKA defaults). The choice of TF-IDF, and of word vs character n-grams for Malayalam and Manglish, is our design decision and should be justified with an ablation.

column1: Why spam detection is not phishing detection
column2: Spam is unsolicited bulk messaging, mostly promotional; phishing and scams are deceptive messages aiming at credentials or money. P04 and P05 show these classes are separate and easily confused (P05: all models struggled to separate spam from smishing).

column1: Why English SMS is not Malayalam or Manglish
column2: The corpus is English in Latin script, collected from UK forum posts and volunteer texts. Malayalam script, non-standard romanization (Manglish) and code-mixing change tokenization, spelling variance and vocabulary.
Spam came mostly from a forum and ham from volunteer and thesis texts, so a classifier can partly learn source style. The data are from the 2000s, and scam tactics have changed.

column1: B. Most defensible provisional research direction (no F1 target and no fixed dataset size promised)
Directly relevant vs foundational vs indirect
column2: Closest to the task: P08 (pending full text) and P06 (unverified). Language and model foundations: P12 (data context only), P13, P14, P15, plus the baseline P01. Indirect methods and cautions: P02, P03, P04, P05, P07, P09, P10, P11. No paper in the set is a Malayalam or Manglish phishing study.

Within the reviewed set, nothing evaluates phishing or scam detection on Malayalam script, Manglish or Malayalam-English text with documented provenance and leakage-aware splits. This must be stated narrowly, because search snippets show Dravidian SMS spam datasets that include Malayalam. The defensible gap is phishing/scam-specific, form-aware evaluation, not 'first work on Malayalam'.

column1: What the project can contribute without overstating novelty
column2: (1) A documented labelling protocol and corpus, with each message tagged by form (Malayalam script, Manglish, mixed) and provenance (natural, translated, generated). (2) A controlled comparison of a TF-IDF linear SVM with one multilingual transformer, reported per form with grouped splits. (3) Analysis of spam-vs-scam confusion and of Manglish tokenization.

column1: Is SVM + one multilingual transformer still justified?
column2: Yes as a minimal design. P01 supports a linear SVM as a strong baseline, and P04/P07 show transformer vs classical comparisons are standard. Choose between MuRIL and XLM-R only after a tokenizer diagnostic on a pilot sample, since neither paper shows Manglish phishing results. Also report a trivial baseline, as P01 does.

Usable for sanity checks only: UCI SMS Spam (English) and the Mishra-Soni SMS Phishing set (English). Contextual only: DravidianCodeMix (sentiment/offensive labels), Multilingual Spam Data (machine-translated), the proprietary P08 data, PhishNet Dataset2 (synthetic spam). Candidates to verify: SMSDHL and Dravidian Spam SMS (Malayalam spam labels, not phishing).

(a) Exact label definitions for SCAM/PHISHING vs BENIGN, including where promotional spam and OTP or bank notices belong, with written guidelines and an agreement check. (b) Data sources, consent, privacy and PII redaction. (c) A rule for assigning form tags, and a Manglish spelling-variant policy. (d) Benign and scam messages from comparable channels and periods to avoid source shortcuts. (e) Split design grouped by template, campaign and near-duplicate; no augmentation before the split. (f) Per-form metrics with seeds and intervals. (g) Verify P06 and P08 languages and the Dravidian SMS resources.
